attacks.claim: Section 3 makes Cirrus Cloud the single sync backend in app 5.0 and archives the stride-server Docker image, contradicting the charter's promise that users can self-host sync and own their data. The ~3,000 self-hosted instances have no supported sync path after 5.0.
attacks.evidence: "after which Cirrus Cloud becomes the single sync backend and the stride-server Docker image is archived."

attacks.claim: The server component is proprietary and hosted-only, and the client SDK is a closed prebuilt binary under a commercial license. Once the local store and sync format are Cirrus-specific, self-hosters and users have no compatible backend and no documented exit route.
attacks.evidence: "the server component is available only as the hosted Cirrus Cloud service." / "distributed as a prebuilt binary (iOS xcframework, Android AAR) under the Cirrus commercial license"

attacks.claim: All ~90k users' sync depends on one commercial vendor whose free tier is only 10k devices above current MAU, with no contractual guarantee or fallback if pricing, terms, or availability change.
attacks.evidence: "Pricing: free up to 100k monthly active devices; our 90k fits the free tier."

attacks.claim: Precise GPS tracks and workout data move to a third-party processor with no stated consent, opt-in, privacy notice update, or data processing terms, and self-hosting users are moved silently.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: any consent prompt, privacy notice update, data processing agreement, or opt-in for Cirrus Cloud; "Cirrus replicates to Cirrus Cloud when connectivity returns."

attacks.claim: No hosting region, jurisdiction, or cross-border transfer terms are stated for location and health-adjacent data sent to Cirrus Cloud.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: no region, jurisdiction, or data processing agreement stated for Cirrus Cloud

attacks.claim: Replicating GPS and health-adjacent workout data to a commercial processor has no stated lawful basis, processor terms, or privacy notice update under GDPR/CCPA-type regimes.
attacks.evidence: "schema mapping (workouts, laps, GPS tracks, gear)" / ABSENT: lawful basis, processor terms, privacy notice update

attacks.claim: Shipping a closed-source commercial binary in an MIT-licensed app is not analyzed for license compatibility or redistribution terms, and it reduces users' ability to audit code handling their data.
attacks.evidence: "distributed as a prebuilt binary (iOS xcframework, Android AAR) under the Cirrus commercial license"

attacks.claim: Account deletion covers only the Cirrus user record and synced records; it does not address the on-device stride-backup-v3.db (full pre-migration data kept 30+ days), Cirrus-side backups or logs, or whether deletion reaches replicated copies.
attacks.evidence: "Account deletion removes the Cirrus user record and all synced records via the Cirrus admin API within 30 days." vs "the backup is deleted only after 30 days and two successful syncs."

attacks.claim: Downgrade rollback is unsafe: 4.0 writes and syncs to the Cirrus store, but 3.x restores only from the pre-migration backup, so workouts created or edited in 4.0 are silently lost on downgrade. The backup can also be deleted before a downgrade is ruled out.
attacks.evidence: "If migration fails or the user downgrades to 3.x, 3.x detects stride-backup-v3.db and restores from it" / "the backup is deleted only after 30 days and two successful syncs."

attacks.claim: Users have no documented export or migration path out of Cirrus before deletion, and no plan if the vendor is discontinued or unavailable. Data custody is effectively one-way.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: export or exit path from Cirrus; "Account deletion removes the Cirrus user record and all synced records via the Cirrus admin API within 30 days."

attacks.claim: Legacy REST sync and the stride-server image are sunset in 5.0 ('end of next year') with no commitment to keep the image maintained until then and no migration target for self-hosters.
attacks.evidence: "Legacy REST sync is removed in app 5.0 (planned for end of next year)"

attacks.claim: Tombstones expire after 90 days, but nothing states how a device offline longer than 90 days is prevented from resurrecting deleted workouts, or how server-side and backup copies of deleted data are purged.
attacks.evidence: "Deletes are tombstones retained 90 days so an offline device cannot resurrect a deleted workout."

attacks.claim: Tombstones kept 90 days may retain deleted GPS and workout content on the server beyond user intent, and the plan does not say whether tombstones are purged on account deletion or stripped of location content.
The rollout halt condition is crash-free sessions only, while the primary goal is sync correctness. A release could lose or duplicate data while staying above 99.3% crash-free.

The sync success metric is client-reported, and the backup-deletion rule ('two successful syncs') does not define durability. Data could be deleted from the backup before it is confirmed stored on Cirrus.
attacks.evidence: "Sync success rate (client-reported) >= 99.5%" / "the backup is deleted only after 30 days and two successful syncs."

attacks.claim: The 5-week, 3-contributor timeline is not sized for an SDK spike, a migration with rollback, 14 conflict scenarios, a legacy path, and a 500-user beta. Week 2 covers migration plus backup/restore with no sizing.
The 'lost/duplicated workout' 80% reduction target has no baseline and relies on client-reported data, so it cannot be measured against a defined starting point.
attacks.evidence: ""Lost/duplicated workout" issues down 80% within 2 months of 4.0."

attacks.claim: Per-field HLC timestamps and per-record change tracking leak device and edit-history metadata to the server, and the plan does not address this.
attacks.evidence: "per-field last-writer-wins using a hybrid logical clock stamped on device"

attacks.claim: The free-tier fit is asserted without citing vendor terms or confirming usage counting and ToS permit this use at scale.
attacks.evidence: "Pricing: free up to 100k monthly active devices; our 90k fits the free tier."
